items.question: Why do you think prompting alone only gets you so far when building AI agents?
items.object: RL fine-tuning versus prompting for building AI agents
items.answer: Basically, look at OpenAI's deep research agent, right? So they have been telling us to just prompt models, but they ended up using fine-tuning, RL fine-tuning, to actually build this agent, right? And the reason they do this is because objectively, yes, I think the prompting only gets you so far. You want to use RL as a way to teach the model what's good, what's bad, and how to reason through things and so on.

You want to use RL as a way to teach the model what's good, what's bad, and how to reason through things and so on.

items.question: How did your experience on Google's Bard team shape your thesis for starting Bespoke Labs?
items.object: The data-centric thesis behind Bespoke Labs
items.answer: So I was in the extended Bard team, now called Gemini, and one thing was very clear: the role of data, right? So there was a huge difference between where Bard started after the 100-day sprint and then eventually as the model kept improving. There were, of course, some modeling improvements, but everything is all about data: what data recipes we use, how we curate the data, how we filter out data, and so on. I felt like there was a huge missing component around this externally, that people didn't have access to these tools, didn't have access to these insights. I mean, there is also something educational here: people don't spend as much time looking at the data. That's something I want to change. Looking at the data has so much alpha, and working on the data, improving the data, rather than spending time on, “Okay, what's my hyperparameter? How do I change learning rate?” So that's the kind of thesis. Also, my co-founder has been involved in what's called DataComp, and there again the goal is all about how do you curate the data, fix the model, create the best data that improves model performance. So for us it was the shared thesis on the importance of data. That's how we kind of launched Bespoke Labs.

items.question: How do you see the relevance of data-centric AI to improving generative models today?
items.object: Data-centric AI in generative model development
items.answer: Those same ideas are exactly still important. It's just that people somehow seem to have kind of lost the train of thought there. If you look at all the improvements in Llama or everywhere, it's all about the data, right? Even in our case, we have been training a bunch of models, and most of the time all the improvement is coming from data, and then some improvement is on the modeling side.

items.question: Why do you think data curation still matters when people can get things done by prompting models?
items.object: Data curation when using models through prompting
items.answer: A lot of people are prompting models to get things done. But the other component is, how do you evaluate? You still need to curate data. As an example, maybe I'm training a model for a specific question-and-answer generation on my corpus and so on. I can prompt the model and say, “Okay, these are the kind of rules to follow,” but ultimately I want to actually evaluate if this is good. Where do I get the evaluation done, right? Again, I have to take my corpus and curate some data and create the evaluation data set. Data basically plays a role.

items.question: Why do you place so much importance on reading model outputs and doing error analysis beyond measuring accuracy?
items.object: Inspecting model outputs and performing error analysis
items.answer: It's not just data, but tooling around how you visualize data. Sometimes the model is doing something very complex; it's producing a bunch of complex JSON, or you have an agent taking a whole bunch of trajectories. There are no good tools out there to actually just look at the data. You don't need to use it for fine-tuning or anything. Just being able to look at the data and read what's happening unlocks a lot of things. One of the things we think about is that when you're evaluating, you kind of have two steps. One is evaluation, maybe the model is 94% accurate or some number like that. But the second thing you need to do is error analysis. I don't think a lot of people are intimately familiar with this. People just stop at evaluation, but what you really need is evaluation and error analysis, where you see what kind of mistakes the agent or the model is making. You can, to some extent, automate this, but most of the time you have to just read what's happening. Then you realize, “Oh, it's actually making these kind of mistakes,” and you realize it's because the retrieval didn't work or the model is hallucinating, and so on. Then you go back and fix your prompts or fine-tune the model. The data curation actually means tooling to munch the data, filter it, but also being able to visualize, read and annotate. Those are the kinds of things that you need to do.

items.question: Why do you see data curation as the problem to focus on when helping people build custom models?
items.object: Data curation as the bottleneck in building custom models
items.answer: I think, taking a step back, the reason why we work on data curation is not to help with data curation per se, but basically people want custom models and custom agents. If we just look at the model part, and if you are trying to fine-tune a model, if you look at why these projects fail, it's because of the data curation part. The mental model I use is from this book called The Crux by Richard Rumelt, I think. He talks about how you have a gnarly problem and you want to figure out what's the crux or what's the bottleneck that's critical that you want to solve. The example he gives is you want to get to Mars, and how do you build a system around this? You can work on making the rockets faster or all sorts of things, but if you think through what the crux of the problem is, you want to get reusable rockets because the cost is the limiting factor in having a system that sends people to Mars. It helps you figure out what it is that you need to solve. Similarly, for post-training, which people want to do for various reasons, the place where they fail usually is in the data part. That's the reason we started with data and built some tooling around visualization and curation.

items.question: What do you think a data curation tool should handle for someone fine-tuning a model?
items.object: Infrastructure for curating model fine-tuning data
items.answer: If I want to fine-tune a model, I want to basically not worry about the infrastructure around data curation. I should be able to pick and choose different models. I should be able to use structured output to guide different stages of doing the data curation, and then I don't want to worry about retries and failures, especially when I have a million examples that I want to create.
quotes: So if you want to fine-tune a model, you want to basically not worry about the infrastructure around data curation. You should be able to pick and choose different models. You should be able to use structured output to guide different stages of doing the data curation, and then you don't want to worry about retries and failures, especially when you have a million examples that you want to create.

rubrics.text: The response proposes using structured model outputs to guide stages of data curation for fine-tuning.
The response states that a data curation tool should spare users from managing retries when generating fine-tuning examples at large scale.

items.question: How do you think about what a data curation tool like Curator needs to provide?
items.object: Curator as a tool for LLM-based data curation
items.answer: So you could be using an LLM to filter your existing human data, or you could be generating more LLM-generated data. So that becomes the synthetic data, right? In any of these situations, when you have a lot of data you want to curate, or even otherwise, you want a systematic tool that helps you curate data. There are a bunch of tools around just prompting models, like LLM and whatnot, but those are specifically geared toward prompting models and you use them in an online fashion. Here it's to a large extent batch mode, offline working, and you want the data throughput to be high, and also ways to visualize if the data quality is good. All of those together are packaged into what's called Curator. Some components of it are open source, and we have ways to upload the data, view what's happening, and so on. That's a bit on the closed-source side.

items.question: What opportunity did you see in DeepSeek R1's release?
items.object: DeepSeek R1's release and the missing reasoning data
items.answer: DeepSeek R1 happened on MLK Day, I think, in January, and we all woke up to the paper and were like, “This is pretty amazing.” We realized the data set is missing, right? What they did was announce DeepSeek R1 and also the distilled models, 32B and 7B. It's all open model, but the data was not something that they released. Given that we had actually built Curator, which is good at data creation, we were able to quickly get started and start generating a reasoning data set. There weren't many such data sets available, especially high-quality ones. We took DeepSeek R1 and curated our own prompts, similar to prior work that was done, and then we used Curator to generate the answer as well as the reasoning trace. We organized a data set and released this as well as the 32B model that was trained on this. So this was the Bespoke Stratos model, which we pulled off in 48 hours. That was pretty well received, and people realized that this kind of data is important.

items.question: How do you see Open Thoughts and Open Thinker contributing to the development of reasoning models?
items.object: Open Thoughts, Open Thinker, and the progression from SFT to RL
items.answer: What we then did was go back and start to work with a whole bunch of people in the open-source community. There was this community of people doing DataComp, so we all worked together and created this consortium called Open Thoughts and Open Thinker. The goal has been to curate reasoning data that people can then use to train reasoning models. The goal of Open Thoughts has been to create really good-quality data. Open Thoughts is the thoughts of the model, and Open Thinker is the model that we train on top of this. Both have been pretty well received. I think the Open Thinker model, the 32B model, actually beats the DeepSeek 32B model. That was a good achievement for all of us who worked together. The data set has also been used by more than 200 models that we know of. The reason this is all popular and useful is that it's unlocking reasoning, and it's tightly connected with RL. What we did earlier is show how you can use just SFT to unlock reasoning in non-reasoning models. Now the next phase is how do you use RL to further augment this.

items.question: Why are you pursuing RL for tool use in building AI agents?
items.object: Prompt-based agent building and RL for tool use
items.answer: That's the other work we have been doing at Bespoke: using RL to make the model reason through things, and specifically we were targeting tool use because that's one of the key components of building agents. Ultimately we want to help people build agents. The way I see it, right now people are just prompting models, and they have these complex series of prompts. They end up in a prompt hell. What's happening is you put together all these prompts and then something works or doesn't, and you don't know why. It's very fragile.

items.question: How do you understand the role of RL fine-tuning in building reasoning agents beyond what prompting can achieve?
items.object: RL fine-tuning versus prompting for building reasoning agents
items.answer: I think the example I give is basically: look at OpenAI's deep research agent, right? They could have built that agent using prompting o3 or o3 mini or o4, but they ended up using RL fine-tuning. They have been telling us to just prompt models, but they ended up using fine-tuning, RL fine-tuning, to actually build this agent. The reason they do this is because objectively, yes, I think the prompting only gets you so far. It's like giving all sorts of instructions. You want to use RL as a way to teach the model what's good, what's bad, and how to—it's not about following instructions, but the model learns to figure out, “Okay, these are the paths to follow; this is how to reason through things,” and so on. So again, it's about reasoning and reinforcing that thought-trace process.

items.question: What limitation do you see in prompting as a way to build AI agents?
items.object: Prompting as a way to build AI agents
items.answer: So what I see happening with prompting is people prompt models and build agents, but they have no way of completing the feedback loop. You have all these prompts and your agent either worked or it didn't work, and now what do you do with that information? You try telling the agent, “Hey, this didn't work,” but that's just another prompt. You just changed the prompt.
quotes: So what's happening with prompting is people prompt models and build agents, but they have no way of completing the feedback loop.

You have all these prompts and your agent either worked or it didn't work, and now what do you do with that information? You try telling the agent, “Hey, this didn't work,” but that's just another prompt. You just changed the prompt.

rubrics.text: The response identifies the lack of a mechanism for closing the feedback loop from an agent’s outcomes as a limitation of building agents through prompting.
The response observes that telling an agent its attempt failed is itself another prompt change.

items.question: How do you think about reinforcement learning as a way to incorporate feedback into an AI agent?
items.object: Reinforcement learning for incorporating feedback into a model
items.answer: I can use RL to do it. Essentially, the process is baking that feedback into the model that I can then run, as opposed to trying to do that interactively at runtime.
quotes: So you can use RL to do it.
You're essentially saying that the process is baking that feedback into the model that you can then run, as opposed to trying to do that interactively at runtime.

items.question: How do you see the bitter lesson applying to the way we guide AI models through prompting?
items.object: Prompting, reinforcement learning, and the bitter lesson
items.answer: I think this also connects back to the bitter lesson that we are all familiar with. At the end of the day, what the bitter lesson says is you don't want to rely too much on human intuition. You just let the model search and learn, right? That's the whole point. With prompting, we are actually giving the model all sorts of human intuition, saying, “At this stage, this is what you should do; at this stage, this is what you should do.” So that is very brittle. The bitter lesson says, in a way, don't do this, but let the model figure that out by itself. All you need to do is set up three things: the algorithm, the environment in which it's working, and a way to verify and give rewards depending on whether it is doing correctly or not.

items.question: How do you see reinforcement learning improving on complex human-written prompts for AI agents?
items.object: Reinforcement learning versus complex human-written prompts for AI agents
items.answer: I think you just let it learn from the different scenarios. It does all sorts of rollouts, gets the reward, and then it learns how to reason through things. It avoids this pitfall of humans writing all these complex prompts. And again, it helps connect the feedback loop. In the other case, where you have prompts, there is no way to connect the output back; the feedback loop is not connected. Here it implicitly does that.

items.question: How do you see the role of adapting open-source models to enterprise environments as frontier models continue to improve?
items.object: Adapting open-source models to enterprise environments
items.answer: So we don't want to fight that train of improvement. But I think the other thing to think about is what's in distribution and what's out of distribution. All the frontier models, what they are in distribution on is what's happening around the world, but they don't know what's happening inside an enterprise. That is out of distribution for these frontier models. They can never get better on these tasks, and so our hope and what we are pitching is we can build tooling that can be used so that you can take open-source models and they understand your environment, your ecosystem, and they get better at the tasks that you care about.

items.question: How do you think about training an open-source model to use an enterprise's tools?
items.object: Training open-source models to use enterprise tools through reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
items.answer: What happens is they basically have to specify, “These are my tools,” and all sorts of definitions around it. Before you know it, the prompt is very complex and the agent's latency adds up, and it also becomes very expensive. What we are trying to do is help enterprises bake that knowledge into the model. You can take any open-source model. It's like hiring a human, right? I can go in and take a look at what's happening. You can tell me all the things, but maybe I need some training to get used to an enterprise when I start doing work at a company. That's the process you can think of as a combination of reinforcement learning and SFT, to get the model trained in your system so it becomes adept at using your tools.

items.question: Why do you think reinforcement learning has become more practical with today's large language models?
items.object: The role of LLM prior knowledge in making reinforcement learning effective
items.answer: RL has been there for a very long time, maybe 30 years or so, I think, and RL has also been effective. In AlphaZero, RL has been pretty effective. So I think what's happening now is the LLMs. Let's take a step back. If we think of the Shakespeare monkey writing Shakespeare thing, you can have millions or billions of monkeys writing and maybe one will get it right. The whole point of RL is trying things out, and you are also giving guidance on what's good and what's not good. If you throw a ton of compute, then at some point all the things that you needed to get right—you find your monkey in a haystack. You can find your monkey and you can also train it, but it's just going to be very expensive. What's happening now with LLMs is you don't need a monkey; you can actually train a human. They come with world knowledge, so you don't need to throw in lots of compute. You can use a lot less compute. That's what I think we are seeing. Let's break this down into three things: the algorithm—there have been many algorithms, like PPO, actor critic, and whatnot. People are using GRPO, which to a large extent is similar to existing algorithms, but it does a few things, a few tricks. Then we have the environment, and verification and reward shaping. The prior knowledge is what has changed: these LLMs come with prior knowledge, so the number of rollouts, the number of trial and errors that the model does, isn't millions of things it has to try, but hundreds of things. These models are now generally very capable, and you just nudge them in the right direction, use GRPO, set up the environment, and use a reasonably good reward model or reward shaping. That's the huge unlock that DeepSeek also showed, and people have been doing this at the frontier labs for a while.

items.question: How do you see the current stage of reinforcement learning with LLMs through the comparison between AlphaGo and AlphaZero?
items.object: The AlphaGo–AlphaZero analogy for reinforcement learning with LLMs
items.answer: AlphaZero is completely trained from scratch, so it uses a lot more compute. Whereas AlphaGo starts from some sort of SFT, some sort of human intuition that's baked in. That's what we have now: an AlphaGo moment. You take these LLMs; they kind of understand the world. They have been SFTed and whatnot. It's a reasonable starting point, and then we are able to do things that we wanted to do. I think this is what David Silver and Rich Sutton have written in The Era of Experience: eventually we will move to AlphaZero, where we are not bounded by human intuition. You don't need so much SFT and human-curated data, and it just learns itself what it needs to do.

items.question: What have you learned about designing rewards for reinforcement learning agents?
items.object: Reward shaping for reinforcement learning agents
items.answer: What we have found is that you are giving it either a positive reward, say plus one when it gets the answer right, or a minus one. Sometimes we do see that the model does what's called reward hacking. The agent finds a shortcut to get the reward that we are promising it by not actually doing the things it needs to do. That's where some form of reward shaping is needed: you try to figure out how to actually reward the model. But at least in our recent work, we found that the simpler the reward, the better it is. Maybe this is some form of Occam's razor. We started with a very complex reward procedure, saying if it follows the specific format of tool calling we give this much reward, and if it gets to the right answer we give it this much reward. If not, then we had this complex system. It wasn't really needed. Ultimately we found that having something much simpler works well.

items.question: What do you see as an interesting open question in designing rewards for training a deep research agent?
items.object: Reward design for deep research agents
items.answer: There's a lot more work. I think the interesting question now is, if you are training a model like a deep research agent, how do you design rewards there? Do you reward the intermediate if it gets something intermediate also correct, or do you just give the final reward saying, “Did it find what I'm looking for or not?”

items.question: Why do you find reinforcement learning easier to work with than supervised fine-tuning for teaching agents to use tools?
items.object: Reinforcement learning versus supervised fine-tuning for teaching agents to use tools
items.answer: For SFT, you have to get all sorts of data, maybe tens of thousands of examples, saying, “This is my question; this is how the tool call should have been,” and so on. That gets complex and cumbersome. If you imagine the agent is supposed to do multi-turn, for a given prompt it has to call multiple tools, then it comes back with the result, and based on the result it has to call something else. This becomes very complex to get the data for doing SFT. What we found is RL is much nicer to work with because you don't need as much data. In that particular case, all we needed was 100 good-quality examples instead of tens of thousands, and you don't need the full demonstrations. The fact that the models have good prior knowledge means they are able to come up with reasonable attempts, so you just need the prompts and a way to verify if the answers are good. RL made it much easier for us to train these agents compared to SFT. That's the main finding and the main thing we're excited about.

items.question: How do you approach training a tool-using agent with reinforcement learning?
items.object: Training tool-using agents with reinforcement learning
items.answer: In RL, what you need is a prompt and an environment where the agent is trying things out, and a way to verify if the answer is right or not. In SFT, all you need is, “Here is my prompt. Here is the actual response that it should be doing.” We don't need that in RL. We have a bunch of prompts that say, “Book a flight ticket on this day, when the cost is cheaper,” blah, blah, blah. That's one example prompt. The agent acts in a specific environment where it's able to try things out. It's a fake environment; it's not actually booking flights. You need to construct these realistic environments, set up the rewards, verify if things are working, put it all together and run it with GRPO. The way the GRPO algorithm works is it takes one of the prompts and has what's called a rollout. Eight different times it tries, and then for each of them you get a reward. Based on the reward, you compute what's called an advantage, and that tells you which direction you should update the model. The tries are responses to the prompt.

items.object: Compute requirements of reinforcement learning compared with supervised fine-tuning

items.question: Why do you want AI engineers who currently rely on prompting to have access to model-training tools?
items.object: Democratizing model-training tools for AI engineers
items.answer: Our goal is to actually democratize access to these tools. Even with data curation, all the frontier labs have good tools that people should have access to so they can train good models as well. They don't have to rely on OpenAI training the best model and then use that. They should be able to train good models for their use cases, so it's cheaper and better quality. Similarly, there is an opportunity to democratize tooling. Our ultimate goal is this is not restricted to researchers, but all the AI engineers who are now prompting should be using these tools to build agents. For me, that's my personal goal: not have people spend so much time on prompting, but actually fine-tune and do these things. I'm slightly biased because I'm an ML engineer and all of this is intellectually stimulating, to actually fine-tune a model rather than prompt. But in general, I feel like there are a lot of benefits to doing this, so I want to make it accessible to as many people as possible.

items.question: How do you assess what reinforcement learning improved in your tool-calling model?
items.object: Evaluating reinforcement learning for tool calling
items.answer: We took a base model, a Qwen-Ben Instruct model, 7B, and then we do RL. There is qualitative and quantitative evaluation. We took a tool-calling data set called BFCL; it's a benchmark. You split it into train and test, and then you can see how the model does after you fine-tune. That's one thing, and you can also look qualitatively at what it does. We did see that the reasoning actually improves. The non-fine-tuned model would just make some kind of silly mistakes, or it was mostly doing just single-turn. After you did RL, it became able to do multi-turn tool calling. It would call one tool, look at the response, and then decide, “Based on this, I need to call a different tool.” That was the qualitative evaluation we did, which was quite nice to see: the model is picking this up without us having to curate any of the data. That was our way of evaluating. The other thing we could have done is actually SFT and then compare SFT with RL, but we didn't have the data. This whole benchmark is about 200 examples, so we would have needed a lot more examples. We did do some SFT work before; we were running into all sorts of issues, so we didn't really do SFT to compare RL against SFT here.

items.question: Why do you see multi-turn tool use as necessary for some AI agent tasks?
items.object: Multi-turn tool use by AI agents
items.answer: Let's take an example of asking the model to delete a file in a specific folder. It might attempt to try to delete it directly, or it may say, “Let me first see where I am.” It might execute pwd, and then based on that say, “I now need to go to that folder,” so cd to that folder and then delete. So this is multi-turn. There are many cases where we need multi-turn. You cannot do it in a single turn because you need to wait for the response. Similarly, in deep research, the model first needs, for your query, to break it down into multiple subqueries.

items.question: Why do you train a dedicated model like MiniCheck to check for hallucinations?
items.object: MiniCheck and grounded factuality
items.answer: The reason we train it is it's often done today just using general models. To give context, MiniCheck is a model that is trained to detect hallucinations. It's a specific problem called grounded factuality. If you take, especially in RAG systems, a context which the model looks at and produces an answer or basically a claim, this particular model is good at checking if this claim is supported by this context or not.

items.question: Why do you see MiniCheck as a useful alternative to general-purpose models for checking whether a response is supported by its context?
items.object: MiniCheck
items.answer: People use GPT for whatever it is. The advantage of using the MiniCheck model is we measure it on a benchmark and it's actually better than GPT-4o in this task. It's way cheaper because it's a 7B model. GPT-4 is, I don't know, how many parameters. It also has latency of 100 milliseconds. In fact, if you use a modern GPU, maybe it's even smaller. It can be used as a guardrail because of its latency, or if you have a lot of data, it can go through it and get a faithfulness metric and things like that. The reason we train this is it's useful in data curation, where you are curating data and generating a lot of synthetic data, and so you want to filter out bad-quality data. That's the reason we trained this, and also to showcase that distillation actually works. This model is distilled, and it outperforms the teacher model. It's also a proof of concept that fine-tuning works. People are very reluctant to fine-tune models, but this is another way to showcase that it works.

The response states that the distilled MiniCheck model outperforms its teacher on checking whether responses are supported by context.

items.question: What do you see your chart question-answering model MiniChart as demonstrating about the value of data curation?
items.object: MiniChart
items.answer: MiniChart is similar: it does Q&A on charts, and we are able to train a 7B model. It's much better than existing 7B models. It achieves the level of Claude 3.5 and Gemini 1.5. Again, the goal is to show that good-quality data and data curation helps. We used a lot of synthetic data and trained that model.
quotes: MiniChart is similar: it does Q&A on charts, and we are able to train a 7B model. It's much better than existing 7B models. It achieves the level of Claude 3.5 and Gemini 1.5. Again, the goal is to show that good-quality data and data curation helps. We used a lot of synthetic data and trained that model.

rubrics.text: The response presents MiniChart reaching Claude 3.5 and Gemini 1.5 performance with a 7B model as evidence of the value of high-quality curated training data.

items.question: How do you think MiniChart should handle answering questions about complex charts?
items.object: MiniChart’s approach to answering questions about complex charts
items.answer: You take a complex chart; it can be an infographic, all sorts of things happening there. Typically, you cannot convert it into markdown. People try to do that, but that doesn't work, so you need a vision language model. These become expensive, and we have this model which is pretty good. We have a playground on our website where people can upload and see what the model does. It's able to answer questions. It's able to do math. You can ask it, “What's the average across however many quarters?” It does all sorts of math. The next thing we are thinking is that it should be able to use tools. In this case, the model itself is doing the math, which can sometimes be error-prone. We can have a situation where the model says, “In order to compute the average, I get these numbers,” and then it calls the tool to get the average and gets back the response. That's something we'll be doing in the future.

items.question: How do you see MiniChart's role within an AI agent?
items.object: MiniChart as a tool for AI agents
items.answer: MiniChart is slightly different in that it is a useful model in itself, a useful tool for an agent. I go back to the deep research agent: it knows how to do web search and things like that, but it also knows when there is a graphic that this is the specific model it needs to call. Similarly, when we want to build an agent that does a whole bunch of things, if it encounters a graph, it's going to call this model.

items.question: How do you think about building a business model for your startup AI lab?
items.object: The business model for his startup AI lab
items.answer: We are definitely thinking through how to get revenue. Ultimately our goal is to build a product that makes recurring revenue. More than consulting, we do have design partnerships which help us build the right kind of tooling, the right kind of models, the right kind of things we need to build. That's something we are doing. Then of course we have a bunch of tooling now on data curation, and we are also building things on RL and so on. That's something we will be monetizing in terms of future directions.

items.question: How do you see reinforcement learning differentiating your approach to building AI agents?
items.object: Reinforcement learning as an approach to building AI agents
items.answer: We are focusing on RL. Basically, perfecting how to do RL and build agents. That's where we get a lot of traction and pull from people trying to build agents. They are frustrated prompting models. We are building a whole bunch of tooling on how to do RL effectively to build agents. That's our differentiating factor because everybody else is building agents by prompting. We are building an ecosystem of good models as well as good tooling, everything put together. We want to make it easy for people to build agents. We are also building some agents ourselves, so it's the full package there.
